sentences.text: In the north of Sweden, above the Arctic Circle, there is a village called Jokkmokk.
In winter, the sun comes up at ten in the morning and goes down at one in the afternoon, and for most of the day the sky is a deep blue that turns to black.
This is where Nell's grandmother lived, in a small red wooden house on the edge of a frozen lake.
And this is where Nell spent Christmas when she was ten years old.
Her grandmother — Farmor Astrid — was small and quiet and had white hair braided down her back.
She spoke English carefully, with pauses, the way people do when they are translating from another language in their head.
The house was warm inside.
There was a wood stove and a rug made of reindeer hide and a shelf full of small carved wooden animals.
Farmor's cat, whose name was Måns, slept in a basket by the fire.
On Nell's first evening, after they had eaten and washed the dishes, Farmor pulled up two chairs to the stove and said, "There is a story I need to tell you."
Nell settled in with a blanket.
"Our family," said Farmor, "has an agreement.
It is very old.
It goes back to my grandfather's grandfather, who was a sailor and who was almost lost at sea one winter, and who was saved by a light he saw in the forest."
"A light in the forest?
On the sea?"
"He had come ashore.
He was lost.
He was going to die of cold.
The light led him home.
When he got to the door of his own house, the light turned into a white fox.
A small fox, with amber eyes.
It looked at him for a long moment.
Then it went back into the trees."
"After that," Farmor went on, "the fox came sometimes, in winter.
Always when the north wind blew for three nights without stopping.
On the third night, the fox would come to the door.
And a gift had to be left for it."
"A gift?"
"Something small.
Something the family had made or found or valued.
My grandfather always left a coin.
His mother left a piece of bread.
My father left a feather.
It did not matter what the gift was, as long as it was given honestly."
"And if you didn't give one?"
Farmor looked at the fire.
"Then the fox took something else," she said.
"That is what the story tells."
Nell was not sure if she believed the story.
It sounded like the kind of story grandmothers told to make winter feel important.
But that night, when she was in bed under her thick duvet, she heard the wind begin.
It was not an ordinary wind.
It came out of the north and it whistled through the trees and it made a sound around the corners of the house like someone humming a long, low note.
Nell got up and went to the window.
The moon was up.
The snow in the yard was bright as day.
And there, in the snow, close to the front door, were small tracks.
Fox tracks.
Fresh.
